Appendix A | JavaScript Game Maker Cheat Sheet

20.11 Plan before choosing code

Build the scene structure → Style the scene → Program game behavior. Choose the job first, then the tool. JavaScript can help with all three jobs in canvas and 3D games.

Step Prepare or change Quick check
Build the scene structure HTML groups and controls; canvas or 3D objects; level layout and game data. Are the needed parts present and arranged sensibly?
Style the scene CSS; canvas drawing; sprites; materials, lights, and readable feedback. Can a player recognize the goal, controls, and important objects?
Program game behavior Input, state, decisions, movement, collisions, scoring, and restart. Does one action produce the predicted result?

Keep these patterns nearby while you build. Examples with ... are sketches, not finished code.

Tool Example Use it when…
Variable let score = 0; Stores a value that can change.
Constant const speed = 4; Names a value whose binding you do not plan to reassign.
Decision if (score >= 10) { ... } Runs code only when a condition is true.
Function function jump() { ... } Names a reusable action.
Random Math.floor(Math.random() * 10) Makes an integer from 0 to 9.
Array const enemies = []; Stores a collection.
Loop for (const enemy of enemies) { ... } Processes items one at a time.
Timer setInterval(move, 1000); Repeats on a time interval.
Animation requestAnimationFrame(loop); Runs the next animation frame.
Canvas ctx.fillRect(x, y, w, h); Draws a rectangle.

Appendix B | Debugging Checklist

20.12 Find the stage that needs attention

Use Build the scene structure → Style the scene → Program game behavior to narrow down a problem. Check the earlier stages before changing a rule that depends on them.

Stage Ask Try
Build the scene structure Does the needed element or world object exist? Check HTML IDs, file paths, object positions, and level data.
Style the scene Is it visible and readable? Check size, color, display rules, camera, lighting, and hitbox overlays.
Program game behavior Is the action received and the state updated? Log input and values; trace one update; check collision, scoring, and restart.

Predict the result of your fix, change one thing, and compare what happens with your prediction.

Appendix C | Optional Next Step: Phaser

20.13 Keep your development flow

Build the scene structure → Style the scene → Program game behavior still guides a framework project. First decide which objects, controls, and state the scene needs; then choose sprites, sizes, placement, and readable feedback; then connect input, movement, collisions, and game rules. Test one small action before expanding the game.

These are planning steps. Phaser’s preload, create, and update are runtime responsibilities: create may both build and style objects, while update may change their behavior and appearance. The two sequences do not match one-to-one.

Once you understand variables, functions, state, animation, and collision in plain JavaScript, you can explore a game framework such as Phaser. A framework provides tools for game tasks so you can spend less time on low-level drawing code.

Keep the ideas you already know: loading resources, creating the world, and updating the game. The sketch below names those responsibilities. It is not a complete Phaser project and does not load or configure the library.

// Conceptual Phaser-style structure
function preload() {
  // Load images and sounds
}

function create() {
  // Create the game world
}

function update() {
  // Run once per frame
}

Explore the official Phaser website for its documentation and examples.

Appendix D | Check Your Game-Making Skills

20.14 Explain your three steps

For every exercise or challenge, describe Build the scene structure → Style the scene → Program game behavior. If you reused a stage, explain why it was already suitable.

Step Evidence to collect
Build the scene structure A labeled sketch or screenshot showing the page groups or world objects.
Style the scene One design choice and how it helps the player read or use the scene.
Program game behavior One predicted action, the observed result, and an explanation of the state or rule involved.

Choose your next improvement from that evidence, then repeat the three-step flow.

A working game is only part of what you have learned. Use this checklist to collect evidence that you understand your program and can improve it.

Skill I can show that… My evidence
Playable game My controls and core rules work. A short playthrough.
Code understanding I can explain important variables, decisions, functions, and state. Three annotated code examples.
Debugging I can describe a bug and how I investigated it. A before-and-after debugging note.
Modification I can make a small change without replacing the whole program. One change and its test result.
Game design Another player can understand the goal and feedback. A playtest observation and improvement.

Appendix E | Your Game Lab

20.15 Remix with the three-step guide

Use Build the scene structure → Style the scene → Program game behavior for every Game Lab experiment. Inspect the existing project first and keep any stage that already supports your change.

Step Where to look What to check
Build the scene structure Project index.html, scene setup in main.js, and any level data such as Robot Orchard’s level.json. Required controls, objects, starting positions, and state exist.
Style the scene Linked styles in games/shared/, canvas drawing, sprite assets, or 3D materials and lights. The player can distinguish the changed object and understand its feedback.
Program game behavior Input handlers, update functions, collision helpers, and game rules. The change behaves as predicted during play, at boundaries, and after restart.

For example, a new collectible needs a place and a stored collected state; a recognizable appearance; and a collection rule that updates the score only once. Add and test one collectible before making a whole new level. A color-only exercise can reuse the existing scene and rules, then check that the new color remains readable during play.

20.16 Start a local server

The first one-file games can open directly from your drive. The Game Lab projects are different: their HTML pages load JavaScript modules, shared code, artwork, level data, or 3D models. A local web server gives the browser a safe way to ask for those files.

How you open a page Address you may see Best for
Double-click an HTML file file:///... A simple, complete one-file game.
Start a local server, then open its address http://127.0.0.1:8000/... This book’s multi-file Game Lab projects.

A server is not automatically a giant computer far away. Here it is a small program running on your computer. 127.0.0.1 is a special address that means “this computer.” It does not publish your work on the internet.

20.16.1 One-time setup: install Node.js

The Game Lab’s server is included in this textbook. It uses Node.js, a free program that can run JavaScript outside the browser. You do not need to install npm packages or find another web-server app.

Because installing software can require a password or school permission, do this step with a parent, teacher, or other adult:

  1. Visit the official Node.js download page.
  2. Choose the LTS installer for your computer. LTS means “long-term support,” a version chosen to stay dependable for longer.
  3. Open the downloaded installer and follow its instructions. Keep the normal choices unless your school gives different instructions.
  4. Close and reopen any Terminal, PowerShell, or Command Prompt windows. Type node --version and press Enter. A version number means Node.js is ready.

20.16.2 Easiest way: double-click the Game Lab launcher

Keep this textbook’s folder structure intact. Open the extracted Quarto_Doc folder.

  • On macOS, double-click start-game-lab.command.
  • On Windows, double-click start-game-lab.bat.

The launcher starts the local server and opens the Game Lab in your usual browser. Leave its window open while you play. To stop the server, close that window or press Ctrl+C in it.

If your computer asks for permission to run the launcher, do not ignore the warning. Ask an adult or teacher to check that the file came from this textbook folder. If school rules block launcher files, use the terminal method below.

20.16.3 Terminal method

Open a terminal in the extracted Quarto_Doc folder. On macOS, use Terminal; on Windows, use PowerShell or Command Prompt. If your terminal is somewhere else, use cd to move into that folder first:

cd "/path/to/your/Quarto_Doc"

Replace /path/to/your/Quarto_Doc with the real location on your computer. Then run:

node scripts/serve.mjs

Leave that terminal window open while you play. Open http://127.0.0.1:8000/games/ to choose a project. Open http://127.0.0.1:8000/preview.html to read the included HTML edition. Stop the server with Ctrl+C. The server listens only on your computer’s loopback interface; it is a development tool, not a public hosting service.

No npm install is needed. If the terminal says that node is not recognized or not found, repeat the Node.js setup with an adult or teacher.

The browser’s trip is simple: browser asks for main.js or an image, the local server finds that file in the textbook folder, and the browser receives it. Double-clicking an HTML file is not enough for these module-based projects because module, model, and JSON loading use browser requests. Another local static server also works, but keep the whole folder tree together.

20.17 Choose a project

Project Chapter Controls and purpose
Collision Playground 13–14 Move with arrows/WASD or drag the player. Switch shape and turn wall blocking on or off.
Robot Orchard 13–16 Start; move with A/D or left/right; jump with Space/up/W; P pauses, R restarts, H shows hitboxes. Collect every gem and enter the portal.
Robot Island Explorer 17–18 Move with arrows/WASD; drag to orbit the camera; scroll to zoom. Collect four gems. Crates are decorative in this non-physics project.
Rapier Drop Lab 19 Drop again; orbit the camera; show colliders. Compare three bounce coefficients.
Marble Quest 20 Start; arrows/WASD move the marble; P pauses, R restarts, H shows colliders. Collect five gems and enter the gate. Falling costs a life.
3D Asset Workshop 18 Change the robot body’s color, orbit the view, and export your own GLB file.

Click the game canvas before using keys. Movement controls are intentionally world-relative in the 3D games: W/up moves toward negative Z even if you rotate the exploration camera. The lab also supplies large onscreen controls where movement is needed. These are useful alternatives, not a claim that every canvas interaction is fully accessible to every player.

20.18 Find the source you need

chapters/               The textbook's Quarto chapters
figures/                Original diagrams with editable SVGs used by Chapters 13-20
games/
  index.html            Game Lab menu
  collision-lab/        Shape detection and wall-response experiment
  robot-orchard/        Complete 2D game and editable level.json
  three-explorer/       Three.js exploration without physics
  physics-lab/          Rapier bounce experiment
  marble-quest/         Complete 3D physics game
  asset-workshop/       GLB model customization and export
  shared/               Input, loops, collision helpers, styles, 3D setup
  assets/               Original SVG, PNG, GLB, JSON, and WAV files
scripts/                Local server, dependency download, book builders
start-game-lab.command  macOS double-click launcher
start-game-lab.bat      Windows double-click launcher
tests/                  Automated checks for reusable game logic

The complete project folders are the source of truth for runnable code. Snippets in the chapter explain selected pieces; some are deliberately simplified to focus on one idea. Do not append every snippet to main.js as though they were all additional instructions.

20.19 Use the custom asset pack

The supplied robot sprite has four 64 by 64 frames. Edit the SVG source while keeping the 256 by 64 sheet size, or replace it with a PNG sprite sheet and update the image path. An image’s transparent space is not a collider. Keep the player’s physics dimensions separate from the drawing dimensions.

The 3D pack contains robot.glb, crate.glb, and gem.glb. model-specifications.json records their origins and dimensions. They are rigid models without a skeleton or animation clips. Move and rotate their roots in the game; use a different animated GLB only after adding animation handling.

The artwork and short collection sound were created for this project. The asset permission statement in games/assets/ASSET_LICENSE.md allows reuse and modification. It does not grant rights to unrelated images, commercial characters, or library code. When adding downloaded assets, record their source and license.

20.20 Make the 3D projects available offline

By default, import maps load Three.js 0.180.0 and Rapier’s compatibility package 0.17.3 from jsDelivr. These fixed versions keep the four 3D projects on the same dependency set. On a computer with internet access, Python 3 can download the two packages and switch the import maps to local copies:

python3 scripts/vendor-dependencies.py

On Windows, py scripts/vendor-dependencies.py may be the appropriate command. Keep games/vendor/ with the project when copying it to another computer. Test every 3D page once while offline. Continue using the local server even after downloading the dependencies.

The script retains the packages’ licenses. To switch the pages back to their original CDN imports, use python3 scripts/vendor-dependencies.py --cdn. Downloading packages and changing browser caches can be subject to your computer or network’s restrictions.

20.21 Debug in layers

A blank page is not automatically a game-logic bug

Check the page’s visible error message and then the browser console. First check that the local server is running. Next check file paths and dependency requests. For a 3D page, check WebGL2 support and hardware acceleration. Only after the scene loads should you investigate collisions and score rules.

Symptom Check first
A model or JSON file is not found Keep the folder tree together; check spelling, capitalization, and the Network panel.
A 3D page reports a module error Check internet/CDN access or run the optional dependency-download script.
The ball passes through the ground Check that both relevant shapes have colliders, dimensions match, and the physics world is stepped.
The player stops far from a wall Show hitboxes/colliders; compare the collision shape with the visible asset.
A score increases repeatedly Collect only once and ignore end-of-overlap events.
Movement continues after changing tabs Clear input state on blur and pause the game appropriately.
Restart makes the game faster Look for a second animation loop or duplicated event listeners.
Sound is silent Enable the sound option after starting; browser audio rules may require a user action.

20.22 Test before changing several things

From the project root, run:

node --test tests/*.test.mjs

These tests check reusable collision and game-rule functions. They do not replace playtesting, visual review, or running Rapier’s actual simulation. After editing a rule, test its edge cases and then play the game. Make one change at a time so the result teaches you something.

References and Further Learning

Use these resources when you want another explanation or a new project idea. Follow the main chapters first; some external material assumes more programming experience.

Resource Explore it for…
MDN: Game development tutorials More browser-game projects and explanations.

MDN: Canvas API Drawing shapes and working with a canvas.
MDN: Number inputs Input constraints and validation.

MDN: JavaScript modules Organizing JavaScript across files.
Eloquent JavaScript, by Marijn Haverbeke Deeper JavaScript study after you have experience.
Phaser A possible next step in browser-game development.

Dynamic 2D and 3D game development

The companion projects are original examples. The following official documentation explains the browser and engine APIs used in Chapters 13-20. Read the short examples in the book first, then consult an API page when you need to check a specific behavior.

  • MDN: 2D collision detection - geometric overlap tests and the difference between simple bounding shapes and visible artwork.
  • MDN: requestAnimationFrame - browser animation callbacks and timestamp-based motion.
  • MDN: Canvas drawImage - cropping sprite sheets and drawing images.
  • MDN: import maps - how module names map to URLs.
  • Three.js: WebGLRenderer - rendering a scene with WebGL2.
  • Three.js: GLTFLoader and GLTFExporter - loading and exporting the supplied custom 3D assets.
  • Three.js: OrbitControls - inspecting a scene by orbiting the camera.
  • Rapier: JavaScript getting started - initialization and package choices.
  • Rapier: rigid bodies, colliders, and advanced collision detection - motion, contact shapes, sensors, and events.
  • Rapier: character controller - an optional next step beyond a rolling marble.

The companion project intentionally pins Three.js 0.180.0 and @dimforge/rapier3d-compat 0.17.3; these are selected versions, not a claim about the latest release. Online documentation can evolve independently. Update dependencies deliberately and retest all projects together.
